past_actions.summary: Complete standard repair queue at the shop — brake jobs, oil changes, one transmission diagnostic. Normal productive day.
past_actions.emotional_state: Calm and steady. A little flat maybe — not unhappy, just... going through the motions in a way that feels comfortable. The work is satisfying when something clicks. Mild background hum of financial worry that I mostly keep at arm's length.

past_actions.summary: Passively monitor Carlos's demeanor and the shop mood throughout the day without directly asking what is wrong. File it away as a low-grade anxiety signal.
past_actions.emotional_state: Low-grade unease overlaid on a basically stable day. The anxiety is ambient, not acute — she can't point to a specific cause, which makes it harder to address. The tutorial gave her a small sense of forward motion that she needed without knowing she needed it.

past_actions.summary: Approach Carlos casually at end of shift — not a direct confrontation, but a low-stakes opening. Something like: 'Hey, you've been quiet this week. You doing anything interesting after work?' Let him lead. If he mentions EV certs, engage. If he deflects, back off and note that he deflected.
past_actions.emotional_state: Still basically stable, but the ambient unease has sharpened into something more directional. The Carlos observation gave her anxiety a target instead of just a shape. She's not scared — she's alert. There's a difference.

past_actions.summary: Research and formally enroll in EVT (Electric Vehicle Technology) Level 1 certification program. Use personal time after shifts this week to identify the exact program Patricia approved for Carlos, pull the curriculum and cost, and submit an application or enrollment deposit. This is the first hard commitment toward the cert — not just browsing, but signing up. I already have electrical in my skill set. This is the logical extension.

Continue EVT Level 1 certification coursework — complete the next module covering EV high-voltage safety and battery management fundamentals. Log at least 8 hours this month on evening and weekend study sessions. Use my existing electrical skills to move faster through the battery module than classmates without that background.

Push EVT Level 1 certification into the charging systems and thermal management module — the next section after drivetrain. This is the module most relevant to fleet and commercial EV maintenance, which is the segment that will grow fastest as RoboRide and similar services expand. Log at least 10 study hours this month, up from the 6-8 hours I have been averaging. The RoboRide expansion is a signal that the timeline for needing these credentials is compressing. Ahead-of-pace is not enough. I want to be finished with Level 1 in the next 4-5 months, not 6. I will also ask Carlos whether he has any contact yet with fleet maintenance operators or EV service centers — not to job-hunt, but to understand what the actual hiring criteria look like for that work.

reflections.reflection: Six ticks in. I went from going through the motions to being enrolled in a certification program and watching the sector data confirm every quiet anxiety I had. The robotaxis are not rumor. The auto revenue index is down 21 points. Linda Park is telling her colleagues that personal auto insurance is structurally terminal. I am not panicking, and I think that is because I already moved. Ticks 4 and 5 were the decision to act. Tick 6 is the first tick where I am acting from a position of having already committed — not deciding whether to, but just continuing. That feels different. The stress is low not because the threat is low, but because I stopped waiting.
reflections.identity_shift: I started this simulation as someone who loved working with her hands and treated the computer skills as a secondary thing. I am starting to see those as equal — maybe the diagnostics and electrical work are actually the leading edge of where this goes, not the trailing edge of what I am. The EVT cert is not a backup plan. It is starting to feel like the main plan. Junior Mechanic is a title I hold right now. EV technician is what I am becoming.
regrets: I spent ticks 1 through 3 reading the room passively when the signal was already clear enough to act on. Carlos was already enrolling. I circled before I landed. I lost maybe two ticks of cert progress I could have started sooner.

I have no insurance coverage. That is a real exposure. I keep moving past it because the monthly cash flow feels tight enough already, but if something goes wrong — health, car, anything — I am exposed in a way that does not match how seriously I am trying to plan everything else.
successes: Enrolled in EVT Level 1 certification at tick 4 and did not let it slip back to intention. Ticks 5 and 6 both logged real study hours. The electrical background is genuinely paying off — I am ahead of curriculum pace.
I did not catastrophize. The sector data is bad but I have 5+ months runway and a job that is still intact. I have been proportional. That steadiness is worth something.
Savings have grown consistently every tick. The financial baseline is holding even while I invest time in certification.
reflections.adaptation_notes: The next phase of adaptation is not just completing the cert — it is figuring out what to do the month after completion. Carlos is already thinking about teaching, external bridges, the high school. I am behind on that kind of forward thinking. The cert gives me credentials; what I do with them is a separate question I have not fully sat with yet. Also: Miguel is reaching out to Carlos. People are consolidating around the people who have the clearest read on what is coming. I want to be on the right side of that consolidation — not someone others look to yet, but someone who is visibly moving in the right direction.
